opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real phenomenon, and I understand why it's happening. Over the last few years, language models have shown what scaling a simple objective on internet-scale data can do. A lot of the excitement, the funding, and the talent followed that. If you're a first-year PhD student today, it's very natural to think the main action is in LLMs, and that vision is a solved problem or just a module you plug in.

But I actually think this is a bit of a historical misreading. Vision isn't a sub-problem of intelligence. In many ways it's the foundation of it. Think about how intelligence evolved in animals. Long before language, there was perception: seeing the world, building a model of it, predicting what happens next, acting in it. Language is an incredibly powerful compression of human knowledge, but it's a description of the world, not the world itself. If we want systems that understand physical space, that can reason about objects, causality, and dynamics, and eventually act in the real world as robots or agents, then visual understanding is unavoidable.

There's also a technical point. Language is already highly structured and semantically dense. Every token carries meaning that humans put there. Visual signals are raw, continuous, high-dimensional, and full of redundancy. The question of how to learn good representations from that kind of data, without humans labeling everything, is still largely open. In language we arguably found a recipe that works. In vision, I don't think we've had our "GPT moment" yet, in the sense of a single scalable paradigm that clearly gives you general visual intelligence. To me, that's exciting rather than discouraging. The hardest and most interesting problems are still there.

So my honest feeling is a bit contrarian. When fewer people work on something, that's often exactly when it's a good time to work on it. The people who stay are usually the ones who really care about the fundamental questions, not just following a trend. And I believe the field will come back around. As multimodal models, world models, and embodied AI mature, people will rediscover that the bottleneck is often not the language part but the seeing and understanding part.

What I tell students is: don't think of computer vision as a narrow field about benchmarks like detection or segmentation. Think of it as the study of how a machine can perceive and model the world. Framed that way, it's not shrinking at all. It's becoming more central to the whole AI story.

r001.rationale: The response says vision is the foundation of intelligence and that visual understanding is unavoidable for systems that understand and act in the world.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually don't see it as a crisis, though I understand why it looks like one from the outside. When students ask me whether they should still do vision, I tell them the question itself is a bit of a trap.

What's really happening is that the boundaries are dissolving. Ten years ago "computer vision" was a very clear thing: you worked on ImageNet, on detection, on segmentation, and the community had its own conferences, its own benchmarks, its own culture. A lot of the people who used to call themselves vision researchers are now working on multimodal models, on video generation, on world models, on robotics. They didn't leave vision. Vision got absorbed into something bigger, and the label became less useful.

So if you measure by how many people say "I do computer vision," yes, the number is going down. But if you measure by how much of the frontier depends on understanding visual signals, it's never been higher. Every serious foundation model team is wrestling with how to represent images and video, how to learn from pixels without labels, how to connect perception to action. Those are vision problems. They're just not wearing the old uniform.

I'd also say the field needs this moment. For a long time vision was somewhat insulated. We had our tricks, our architectures, our evaluation habits. The language community came in with scaling, with simple objectives, with very large and messy data, and it forced us to ask uncomfortable questions. Why hasn't self-supervised learning in vision produced the same kind of emergent capabilities we see in language? Why do we still rely so heavily on language as a crutch to supervise visual understanding? I find those questions much more exciting than tuning another detector.

And honestly, when a field gets less crowded, that's often the best time to work on it. The low-hanging fruit is gone, the hype has moved elsewhere, and what's left are the hard, foundational problems. Representation learning from raw visual data, understanding the physical world, spatial reasoning. These aren't solved. If anything, I think the next big breakthrough in AI will come from the visual and physical side, not from text alone. So I tell students: don't ask whether vision is still important. Ask what intelligence looks like when it has to see.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI frontier depends on understanding visual signals and closes by framing seeing as part of what intelligence must do, presenting vision as essential to intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between computer vision as a research label and vision as a fundamental capability. The label may be getting less attention, but the capability is still essential. If we want AI systems to understand and interact with the physical world, they need to perceive it. Language alone doesn’t make that problem disappear.

In fact, some of what looks like people leaving computer vision may be people working on vision under a different name—multimodal learning, robotics, or generative models. So I wouldn’t judge the field’s significance simply by how many people identify themselves as computer vision researchers.

That said, a shift in attention can be useful. It forces us to ask: Are we solving an important problem, or are we just improving a number on a familiar benchmark? For a student, I think that’s the more meaningful question. There are still deep problems in understanding space, motion, and how the world changes. If fewer people are pursuing those questions, that can also be an opportunity to do something distinctive.

r001.rationale: The response calls vision a fundamental capability and says AI systems need it to understand and interact with the physical world, presenting it as essential to intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between computer vision as a label and the problems it studies. Fewer people identifying themselves as computer vision researchers doesn’t necessarily mean those problems have become less important. If we want AI systems to understand and interact with the world, visual understanding is still essential.

What’s changing is where that work happens. Questions that used to sit squarely within computer vision are now part of multimodal learning, robotics, or broader AI research. That can be healthy: the boundaries are becoming more open. But there’s a risk if we start treating vision as a solved component—something you just attach to a language model. Recognizing patterns in images is only part of understanding a physical world with space, motion, and causality.

So I wouldn’t judge the significance of the field by how many people use its name. I would ask whether we’re making progress on those fundamental questions. There’s still a lot to do, and for students, that means there’s room to find important problems rather than simply follow the most crowded direction.

r001.rationale: The response says visual understanding is essential for AI systems to understand and interact with the world, conveying computer vision’s essential role in intelligence.
